sb_prompt: FIND OUT WHAT BOOKS THE OTHER CALLER READS FOR ENJOYMENT OR SELF-IMPROVEMENT.         DO YOU HAVE SIMILAR OR DIFFERENT INTERESTS IN BOOKS?
turns: Hi, I'm glad you called. My name is Sarah, I'm 44, and I work in marketing, though I only have an associate's degree since I took off to raise my kids. How are you doing today?

Oh, hi Sarah! It's great to meet you. I'm actually Alex, I'm 27, and I'm still finishing up my communications degree at the local community college. How did you find the time to raise your kids if you stopped working full-time? I'm always trying to figure out how to balance school and life right now.

That's a tough balancing act, Alex. I actually didn't stop working full-time; I just switched to part-time and freelancing so I could be there for the kids during the week. It kept my mind sharp, and honestly, that's where I found the time to read—late at night when everyone was asleep. I've been trying to get back to reading more for fun since I started freelancing, which is great because I have so much control over my schedule now. What kind of books are you reading while you're in school? Are you sticking mostly to textbooks, or have you picked up any novels or self-help books for enjoyment?

That actually sounds like a great compromise, Sarah. I totally get the part-time hustle; balancing school and work is no joke, especially with the limited hours community college offers. I'm currently diving into a few textbooks for my communications class, but honestly, I've been trying to mix that up with fiction to keep my brain from getting too bogged down. I just finished "The Midnight Library" by Matt Haig, which was really eye-opening about regret and choices, and I'm currently halfway through "Atomic Habits" by James Clear because I'm trying to build a better study routine. Are you reading anything similar for self-improvement, or do you stick more to fiction? I'm curious if your freelancing schedule has you discovering new genres.

Oh, wow, I love that you're reading *Atomic Habits*, Alex! That sounds perfect for a student trying to build a better study routine. I actually picked it up about six months ago when I was feeling a bit overwhelmed with my freelancing workload. It really helped me figure out how to focus better without burning out, which is a big struggle when you're juggling clients and family schedules. As for fiction, I tend to stick to historical fiction or contemporary dramas because they make me feel like I'm living someone else's life, which is a nice escape after a long day. Did you find *The Midnight Library* as impactful as I heard it was? I'm still on the fence about whether I'd want to try that kind of philosophical fiction myself, or do you prefer sticking to practical self-help?

Oh, I think *The Midnight Library* was actually my favorite part of the whole read, honestly. I really resonated with the concept of hitting the reset button on your life when you feel stuck, but since I'm so busy trying to balance my classes and work hours, I probably won't get the chance to read another philosophical novel anytime soon. I'm definitely going to finish *Atomic Habits* this week because I need that practical advice to stop procrastinating on my essays, but I'm definitely sticking to non-fiction for now. Do you find that reading historical fiction helps you understand your own life better, or do you just prefer it as a total escape from reality?

That's so interesting that you resonated with the "reset button" idea, Alex! It actually made me wonder if I should try something like that next time I feel stuck, but honestly, historical fiction feels like the safer bet for me right now. It's less about solving my problems and more about stepping into someone else's shoes to see how they handled things I couldn't control back then. Do you think a book like *The Midnight Library* would help you with your essays, or do you feel like practical advice is the only thing you can get out of a book at your stage in life?

Honestly, I don't think I'd be able to pull the same "reset button" approach as the main character in *The Midnight Library* right now; I feel like I need to be practical and grind through my current obligations first, otherwise I'll just keep spiraling. But that said, your point about stepping into someone else's shoes to understand your own life really stuck with me. I actually just finished *The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck* by Mark Manson, which is basically the exact opposite of *Atomic Habits* in terms of vibe—one is all about building perfect routines, and the other is about learning which things are actually worth stressing over. Have you read any non-fiction that challenged you or changed your perspective, even just a little bit?

Oh, Mark Manson is such a bold choice to pair with *Atomic Habits*, Alex! That sounds like a fascinating clash of philosophies—trying to build a perfect routine while simultaneously telling yourself not to worry too much about it. I haven't actually read that one yet, but I've heard people say it's all about embracing your flaws rather than chasing perfection. Since I'm the type of person who usually tries to plan every little detail in my freelance schedule, I'm wondering if that book was a wake-up call for you or just a nice reminder to relax a bit? Do you find yourself actually applying the "don't give a f*ck" advice, or do you still find yourself stressing over those essays? I'd love to know which book you think is giving you the better tool for right now.

I think the "don't give a f*ck" advice was definitely the wake-up call I needed, Sarah, even though I'm still trying to balance that with the practical habits from *Atomic Habits*. Honestly, my brain keeps oscillating between "just do the hard thing" and "it's okay to be average," so I'm not sure which tool is better yet! I'm definitely still stressing about those essays though, mostly because I'm worried my current GPA isn't going to get me into a good grad program later. Have you ever read a non-fiction book that completely flipped your perspective on work or parenting, something that made you rethink how you spend your day? I'd love to hear your take on that since you mentioned historical fiction earlier.

That's such a relatable struggle, Alex! The tension between "grind harder" and "just let go" is exactly what I faced when I was trying to balance my freelance clients and my kids' schedules. I actually haven't read *The Subtle Art* yet, but reading about your oscillation makes me wonder if maybe I need to loosen my grip a bit more than I usually do. Have you found that the *Atomic Habits* strategies are working for your essays, or is the "don't give a f*ck" approach helping you relax enough to actually start writing without the anxiety? Since you mentioned worrying about your GPA for grad school, does it feel like the pressure is mostly on the academic side, or are you stressed about finding work after you finish too?

Honestly, the "don't give a f*ck" approach is helping me start writing because the anxiety was actually keeping me stuck, but I'm still relying on *Atomic Habits* to keep me on track once I actually start; I don't want to just coast and end up with a bad essay. As for grad school vs. work, I'm feeling the pressure on both sides right now—my GPA is definitely my biggest worry for grad school, but I'm also terrified that if I don't get some real-world experience before I apply, admissions won't even look at my resume. Have you had any luck finding that sweet spot where you can work while still studying hard enough, or do you feel like you just have to choose one path and commit to it fully?

That is such a tough spot to be in, Alex! Balancing the need for high grades with the fear that you lack work experience sounds incredibly stressful. I actually feel like I've found that sweet spot, mostly because my freelance work is so flexible I can tailor it to fit around my kids' schedules, but it's definitely a constant tightrope walk. I don't have the luxury of just "choosing one path" like you might need to do, but I do think focusing on building a portfolio of small projects could help you get that real-world experience without needing a full-time job commitment. Speaking of balancing things, you mentioned using *Atomic Habits* to stay on track once you start writing—have you found specific habits from that book that are actually stopping you from procrastinating, or is it more about the mindset shift from Mark Manson's book that's getting you moving?

That's a great tip about the portfolio approach, Sarah! I think focusing on small freelance projects is exactly what I need right now since I'm terrified my resume will look thin. As for *Atomic Habits*, the one strategy that's actually stopping my procrastination is the "two-minute rule"—I just try to start any task by doing it for literally two minutes, which somehow tricks my brain into getting past the resistance and actually getting my essays started. It's wild how small a shift in mindset can make that big of a difference!

That two-minute rule sounds absolutely brilliant, Alex! I honestly didn't realize there was a specific technique like that in *Atomic Habits*; I just kind of told myself I'd write for ten minutes before I'd give up, which usually led to me doing nothing at all. Knowing there's a concrete way to just "start small" might be exactly what I need to tackle my backlogged freelance proposals without panicking. Do you find that once you start with those two minutes, the momentum carries you through the whole essay, or do you have to keep forcing yourself to keep going? Also, since you're looking into building a portfolio for your resume, have you thought about what kind of small projects you might want to take on first? Maybe something related to your communications major that you could do for a local non-profit or a small business in the area?

That sounds like a great idea, Sarah! I've actually been thinking about volunteering to help organize a local library event or maybe doing some social media copy for a small business to get that foot in the door. The "two-minute rule" is definitely helping me get past the paralysis, though I think I still have to consciously push myself to finish the draft once I've started—sometimes the momentum fades if I don't force myself to keep going. Have you ever thought about using your freelancing experience to build a portfolio like that, or do you prefer just keeping your existing clients happy without adding new work?

That sounds like a fantastic idea, Alex! Volunteering for a library event would be a perfect way to use your communications skills without the pressure of a client deadline, and social media copy is such a in-demand skill for small businesses these days. Regarding the two-minute rule, you're absolutely right that momentum can fade, but I've found that if I just commit to showing up for those two minutes, I rarely stop again—it's almost like the rest of the work just flows naturally. As for my own reading, I actually stumbled upon a book recently called "Educated" by Tara Westover that had a huge impact on how I view learning and family dynamics; it's a memoir, so it's not exactly self-help, but it really made me rethink my own parenting choices and the value of formal education. Have you read any memoirs or biographies that changed how you see your own future, or do you prefer sticking to the practical guides like *Atomic Habits*?

That sounds like an incredible read, Sarah! I actually haven't gotten to *Educated* yet, but I have heard a lot of people rave about how it shifts your perspective on what "education" really means beyond just textbooks. Given that you mentioned it made you rethink your parenting choices, I'm curious if it made you feel like maybe I should be more hands-on with my own studies while I'm in school, or if it was more about how you found the time to raise your kids amidst all that learning? I'm trying to figure out if memoirs are the kind of books that can actually help me navigate the stress I'm feeling right now, or if I should stick strictly to the practical guides like *Atomic Habits* until my grades stabilize.

That is a really deep question, Alex! I think memoirs can definitely help navigate stress, even if they aren't giving you specific checklists like *Atomic Habits*. Tara Westover's story is so powerful because it shows how family dynamics can shape your worldview, and reading it made me realize I wasn't doing my kids a disservice by not sending them to school young, even though my own family wasn't the norm. As for hands-on studies, it definitely changed how I view them—I see them as a privilege now, not just an obligation. Since you're worried about the stress of grad school later, do you think picking up a book like *Educated* would help you reframe your current anxiety, or do you feel like memoirs might just add more emotional weight when you're already overwhelmed with deadlines?

That's a really deep question, Alex! I think memoirs can definitely help navigate stress, even if they aren't giving you specific checklists like *Atomic Habits*. Tara Westover's story is so powerful because it shows how family dynamics can shape your worldview, and reading it made me realize I wasn't doing my kids a disservice by not sending them to school young, even though my own family wasn't the norm. Since you're worried about the stress of grad school later, do you think picking up a book like *Educated* would help you reframe your current anxiety, or do you feel like memoirs might just add more emotional weight when you're already overwhelmed with deadlines?

I think you're absolutely right that it would depend on where I'm at mentally right now. If I'm feeling completely burned out, a memoir might feel too heavy right now, but if I'm in a place where I have some breathing room, it could be exactly what I need to find perspective. I haven't read *Educated* yet, so maybe I should try to squeeze it into my reading list before my grades get any worse. Do you have any other book recommendations that bridge that gap between practical advice and emotional understanding? Something that could help me stay motivated without just being another "how-to" guide?

That sounds like a really wise approach, Alex! I think everyone has different seasons in life where memoirs are too heavy, so waiting until you have that breathing room makes total sense. Since you're looking for something that bridges practical advice with emotional understanding, I'd definitely recommend *The Year of Magical Thinking* by Joan Didion. It's a memoir about her experience with sudden grief, but she writes it in a way that is incredibly analytical and almost instructional about how to get through the chaos without losing your mind. It's not a "how-to" guide, but it's very grounding. Or, if you want something more structured but still deeply personal, try *Maybe You Should Talk to Someone* by Lori Gottlieb—it's a therapist writing about her own therapy while treating a patient, so it has that blend of self-reflection and practical tools you're looking for. Have you heard of either of those, or is there a specific type of memoir you'd prefer to start with?

Oh, those are both fantastic recommendations, Sarah! *The Year of Magical Thinking* sounds incredibly gripping given the analytical angle, and *Maybe You Should Talk to Someone* sounds like exactly that blend of vulnerability and practical insight I'm looking for. I think Lori Gottlieb's book would be perfect since it's a therapist talking about therapy, so it feels like I'm getting an insider's look without having to pay for sessions yet. Honestly, I feel like a book that balances that emotional weight with some actual coping strategies is exactly what I need right now, since my brain is currently oscillating between wanting to cry over *The Midnight Library* and needing to grind through *Atomic Habits* for my essays. Do you think *Maybe You Should Talk to Someone* is more of a memoir or a guide, and have you found it helped you with the stress of balancing your own work and kids, or was it more of a read-for-enjoyment kind of book for you?

That sounds like a perfect fit for your current situation, Alex! Lori Gottlieb's book really does walk that fine line between vulnerability and actionable advice, which is exactly why I think it's going to resonate with you given your oscillation between needing to cry and needing to grind. I haven't found it to be a strict "how-to" manual like *Atomic Habits*; instead, it feels more like a guided conversation where the therapist and the patient figure out the path together. For me, it was less about fixing a specific problem and more about understanding why I was stuck in the first place, which helped me make peace with the chaos of freelancing and parenting. Have you started looking into therapy or counseling yourself, or do you feel like getting a book like that is a great way to explore those heavy emotions on your own before taking that next step?

Oh, that description of Lori Gottlieb's book sounds exactly right, Sarah! It really does feel like having a conversation with someone who understands the struggle rather than just being handed a manual. I definitely haven't started therapy yet—I'm still in that awkward phase where I'm trying to figure out if talking to a human is going to help more than just reading about it. Maybe if *Maybe You Should Talk to Someone* resonates with me, I'll feel ready to take that step. Speaking of balancing emotions and action, you mentioned earlier that you stick to historical fiction or contemporary dramas for your escape. Do you have any specific titles in that genre you're currently obsessed with? I'm kind of craving a novel where the main character just gets to live a totally different life than the one I'm stuck in right now.

Oh, I would love to hear some recommendations! Since you mentioned historical fiction, I've actually been thinking about *The Nightingale* by Kristin Hannah, which is set in Nazi-occupied France and focuses on two sisters with very different responses to war. It feels intense, but it really shows how people navigate impossible situations just to survive and find their voice. Do you have anything like that where the historical context is deep but the story is just incredibly compelling? Or maybe something more modern, like *Less* by Andrew Sean Greer, since you mentioned enjoying dramas that make you step into someone else's shoes? I'm trying to find something that will actually make me laugh a little while I'm studying, rather than just make me cry.

Oh, *The Nightingale* sounds absolutely gripping, Alex! I actually haven't read it yet, but I've heard so many people rave about Kristin Hannah's ability to paint such vivid, emotional landscapes that it definitely fits right into my "historical fiction" bucket. It seems like the kind of book where you lose track of time because the characters are so alive, which is exactly what I need after a week of juggling client deadlines. Since you mentioned wanting something that makes you laugh a little while you're studying, have you picked up *Less* by Andrew Sean Greer yet? I'm curious if you found that as witty and charming as everyone describes, or if it felt a bit too cynical for your taste? If you do end up liking *The Nightingale*, I'd love to hear which sister you relate to more!

That sounds like a perfect plan for my next reading session, Sarah! I'll definitely check out *Less* to see if it delivers on that witty promise without being too depressing, and I might give *The Nightingale* a try if I can find a quiet weekend to immerse myself in it. Speaking of finding time to read, do you have any quick tips for slipping into a historical drama when you're busy? I'm currently trying to carve out 20-minute slots before my classes, so I'm wondering if you've found a specific strategy that works for you when you're freelancing and have kids to manage. Also, since we've been talking about memoirs bridging the gap, have you ever read a biography that made you want to visit a specific era or place in history, or do you prefer staying in the safety of the story?

Also, since we've been talking about memoirs bridging the gap, have you ever read a biography that made you want to visit a specific era or place in history, or do you prefer staying in the safety of the story?

That is exactly the kind of efficient reading strategy I was hoping you'd have some tips on! When I'm juggling clients and kids, I usually go for audio books while I'm doing chores like folding laundry or driving to pick up the kids from school; *The Nightingale* would be perfect for that since the plot is so gripping you won't even notice time flying. As for biographies, I actually just finished *Becoming* by Michelle Obama, which made me instantly want to visit the White House and maybe even the South Side of Chicago, mostly just to understand the different eras she lived through. I think sometimes stepping out of the story and looking at a real person's life journey is just as powerful as fiction, especially when you're trying to figure out what kind of future you want to build. Have you ever read a bio that sparked that kind of travel urge, or do you mostly prefer the comfort of a fictional world where you can control the outcome?

Oh wow, I actually just started *Becoming* a few weeks ago! That makes total sense—there is something so inspiring about hearing her describe the transition from the projects in Chicago to the White House, it really makes you feel like you're traveling through time. I definitely haven't felt that urge to visit a specific place yet; my reading has been much more grounded in my own current reality. I mostly stick to fiction that feels accessible during my lunch breaks at the college, so I'm not sure if a full biography sparks that travel fantasy for me like it does for you. Do you find that reading about real people gives you a different kind of motivation than reading a fictional character who gets to make all the choices you want?

That's such an interesting distinction, Alex! I think reading about real people like Michelle Obama definitely gives you a different kind of motivation because you know the obstacles she faced were actual, tangible hurdles she overcame, which can feel very empowering when you're staring down your own challenges. Fiction, on the other hand, lets you live a life where you have total control over the ending, which is great for escapism but doesn't necessarily prepare you for the messiness of reality. Have you ever found yourself reading a biography just to see how someone handled a specific crisis, like a career loss or a family struggle, hoping their solution would work for you? Or do you prefer sticking to fiction where the "crisis" always resolves in the way the author wants it to?

That is such a great point about real people versus fictional characters, Sarah! I can definitely see how knowing Michelle Obama actually survived those hurdles would feel more empowering than just wishing my fictional character could solve everything instantly. I think I have been stuck in that "fiction bubble" where things always work out perfectly, which is nice for a break, but maybe not helpful when I'm facing real-life deadlines. Have you ever read a biography of someone who failed spectacularly before they succeeded, something that showed the struggle wasn't just a smooth path to the top? I feel like seeing a real-life mess might help me stop feeling so defeated by my own current academic struggles.

That is such a powerful idea, Alex! I actually just finished *Sheryl Sandberg's* biography of her father, but honestly, I think the book that fits your description perfectly is *The Autobiography of Malcolm X*. It doesn't hide the failures or the rough patches; it lays them all bare before showing the transformation. It's intense to read because you see someone who completely lost their way and then had to rebuild everything from scratch, which might give you that realistic perspective on failure that fiction can't offer. Do you think reading about a real-life comeback story like that would help you push through the stress of your GPA, or does knowing the messiness of a real struggle feel too much like looking in a mirror right now?

Oh wow, that sounds incredibly intense, but also really inspiring! I honestly think reading about someone like Malcolm X who had to rebuild their entire identity after such a massive fall would be exactly the kind of "real-life mess" I need to see right now. It might help me realize that my current GPA struggle isn't a permanent mark on my record, but just a chapter in a much bigger story. I'm worried that if I keep reading fiction where everything works out perfectly, I'm going to get too comfortable with my own comfort zone and never face the hard stuff. Do you feel like reading books like that makes the struggle feel more manageable, or does knowing someone else went through it make you feel like your problems are somehow bigger than everyone else's?

Oh, that is such a powerful perspective, Alex! Reading about someone like Malcolm X who rebuilt their entire identity after a massive fall could definitely be the wake-up call you need to stop feeling defeated. I think seeing that your GPA struggle is just one chapter, not the whole story, might take some of that weight off your shoulders. I actually feel like knowing someone else went through the messiness makes my own problems feel a little more manageable because I know it's survivable. That sounds like a really inspiring pivot, Alex! I think diving into *The Autobiography of Malcolm X* could be exactly the wake-up call you need to reframe those GPA worries into a bigger narrative. As for other recent reads, I actually just finished *The Woman Who Sold Wreaths* by Jennifer T. Scott, which is a memoir about grief and healing after the loss of her husband. It wasn't heavy or depressing, but it was so honest about the messy, non-linear process of moving forward that I felt less alone in my own parenting struggles.
